title: Intraday Update: What’s Riling the Markets This Time? - Barron's
text:
Or is it just that old, old adage, “Sell in May and go away”?
You can take your pick.
But one explanation may simply be the rising U.S. dollar, which is up yet again versus major currencies. That makes U.S. assets and exports more expensive to foreigners, while making their assets, and exports, cheaper to us. That can often be a wash.
Since mid-March, when the president appointed Expensive Dollar man Larry Kudlow as his new chief economic adviser, the S&P 500 has fallen about 5%. But that’s only when measured in greenbacks. In a foreign currency such as, say, Swiss francs, it's actually risen over that period.
In other words, what the foreign exchange market giveth, the equity market taketh away (or vice versa).
Blofeld is singing. Future Bond villain Musk chanted “la la la” on Twitter as Tesla (TSLA) beat expectations, but his actions on the conference call with analysts, where he cut people off abruptly , won no fans. Tesla plunged 8% in morning trading.
Among other popular stocks, Apple (AAPL) and Alphabet -aka-Google (GOOGL) were down about 0.7%, Amazon.com (AMZN) 1%, and Netflix (NFLX) 1.6%. Facebook (FB) fell 1.3% as its former pals at Cambridge Analytica closed down in the United Kingdom and prepared to file for bankruptcy.
The administration’s economic team is in Beijing trying to work out a better deal and avoid a damaging trade war. The problem? Surely the more reasonable they sound, the less they’ll scare the Chinese to the bargaining table. (Having President Donald Trump tweet crazy things is probably more effective.)
In any case, the markets aren’t panicking about trade. Yes, soybeans were down 0.5% and oil 0.3% by midday. But the moves are trivial compared to the year’s gains. Hard red wheat was up 0.3% and cattle and hogs more than 1%.
The yield on 10-year Treasuries continued to slide away from the dangerous 3% level, falling another 0.02 percentage point to 2.94%. That ought to make other financial assets more attractive, but may also signal slowing economic growth.
It is possible that markets are worried about the latest twists and turns of the Mueller investigation, as the president’s newest consigliere, Rudy Giuliani, announced that a former consigliere, Michael Cohen, had been paid back for the money he paid to Trump’s former trystee, Stormy Daniels.
Maybe it’s my age, but at this point whenever I hear anything to do with the Mueller investigation I immediately hear the theme tune from Soap playing in the back of my mind. I suspect I am not alone. It will probably take a big development on this topic to really shake markets. Look at what they’ve shrugged off so far. Midday Movers
3D Systems (DDD) is down 6.5% to $9.55 after reporting first-quarter earnings . The 3D printer firm lost three cents a share on revenue of $166 million. Analysts were looking for earnings of two cents a share on revenue of $159.59 million.
Cardinal Health (CAH) is down 18.6% to $52.63 after reporting t hird-quarter earnings , and also hit a new 52-week low today. The health care services company earned $1.39 a share on revenue of $33.63 billion, while analysts were looking for earnings of $1.51 a share on revenue of $33.48 billion. For the full year, Cardinal lowered guidance, as it expects to earn between $4.85 and $4.95 a share, compared with the $5.42 consensus.
NRG Energy (NRG) is up 5.8% to $32.25, at one point notching a 52-week high, after reporting first-quarter earnings. The energy firm earned 87 cents a share on revenue of $2.42 billion, while analysts were expecting earnings of 60 cents a share on revenue of $2.08 billion.
Pioneer Natural Resources (PXD) is down 3% to $190.51 after reporting first-quarter earnings . The exploration and production firm earned $1.66 a share on revenue of $1.27 billion, while analysts were looking for earnings of $1.59 a share on revenue of $1.26 billion.
Prudential (PRU) is down 3.4% to $97.75 after reporting first-quarter earnings . The insurer earned $3.08 a share, above the $2.98 per-share consensus. — Teresa Rivas
